tier_reason: The arXiv preprint (v1, 23 Aug 2026, no venue) compares directly against DuckDB and PostgreSQL 18.4. It states the CPU (2x Xeon Gold 6230) but gives no compiler or flags and links no code, so these are first-party numbers short of A and not peer-reviewed. The ratios above 50x with unstated flags also cap it at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Stateful accelerators: 833x geomean read-only speedup over single-threaded DuckDB on TPC-H SF=20 (the Figure 6 legend says 843x) and 3544x over PostgreSQL (the legend says 3554x). The paper compares this with 34.07x for multi-threaded GenDB and 12.35x for single-threaded Bespoke OLAP. Stateless accelerators reach only 1.99x over single-threaded DuckDB. Under TPC-H RF1/RF2 refreshes the geomean is 733x at 300 s, 629x at 120 s and 375x at 60 s. On the unseen SEC-EDGAR workload (SF=3) it is 102x over DuckDB and 486x over PostgreSQL.
corrections.hardware: Dual-socket server with 2x Intel Xeon Gold 6230 (40 physical cores, 80 hardware threads), 376 GiB memory and a 1 TB NVMe SSD. Query experiments are single-threaded unless noted.
corrections.caveats: The 833x/375x/102x/486x figures are geomeans over workload-specific accelerators that LLMs generated (GPT-5.6 Terra Pro for analysis, DeepSeek V4 Pro for implementation). The accelerators precompute persistent, query-specific auxiliary state such as per-date aggregates, multidimensional summaries and range trees, so many queries become sub-millisecond lookups. JetStream is not a general-purpose engine replacement, and it costs more memory than stateless execution or the GenDB/Bespoke OLAP baselines. The DuckDB baseline is single-threaded by default. The text and the Figure 6 legend disagree (833x vs 843x, and 3544x vs 3554x for PostgreSQL). Ratios exceed the 50x plausibility threshold and no compiler or flags are given, so the tier is capped at C. This is an arXiv preprint (MIT CSAIL authors including Tim Kraska) with no venue stated. No code or artifact link appears on the arXiv abstract page, in the HTML or in the PDF, and none was found by GitHub search.

notes: The abstract, section 3.1 setup and section 3.2 text all check out against the record. The PDF does not name the implementation language; accelerators compile into a shared library loaded as a DuckDB table function or a PostgreSQL extension, so the record's 'C++' is plausible but unconfirmed. has_code=false, license=null and maintenance_status=unknown stay as they are, since there is no repo.
